Approach

Three ideas that run through every project.

They are not product features. They are how we decide what to build, what to test, and what to write down.

01

The thermal path has six boundaries, and no single vendor owns them all.

Cold plate, quick disconnect, manifold, CDU, facility loop, heat rejection. A leak, a fouled plate or a lost megawatt of reuse always happens at a boundary. Someone has to own the whole line.

Read →02

Return-water grade is the first thing that decides whether your waste heat has a buyer.

Not the PUE. The temperature the loop returns at is the first screen for who can take the heat directly: a greenhouse, a district network, a pool, an absorption chiller. Load profile, distance and contract terms come next.

Read →03

A leak is three different failures on three different clocks.

A weld that escaped the factory. A quick disconnect disturbed at commissioning. A hose that ages out in year four. Different owners, different evidence. One checkbox cannot cover them.

Read →
Numbers with boundaries

A number goes out with its condition attached, or it does not go out.

Every performance figure we publish about our own work carries its test condition and its source. Reference figures and calculator assumptions carry a stated basis and a stated limit. A figure we cannot yet state that way does not appear as a headline.

≈55 °CCold-plate loops built on the product platform our founding team created return water at roughly 55 °C.Condition: Secondary-loop return at rated IT load; direct-to-chip cold plate; facility-side approach not included. Delivered by the founding team on their earlier product platform, before NextGenergy. Source: Every Watt Counts, "Waste Heat Becomes an Asset" (June 2026). Verified by: Operating logs; not third-party audited.
50–60 °CFourth-generation low-temperature district heating networks are defined by supply temperatures of roughly 50–60 °C, rising to about 70 °C in winter.Condition: Per the 4GDH definition (Lund et al., 2014: < 50–60 °C, 70 °C in winter); varies by network, season and building stock, and some ultra-low-temperature networks run below 45 °C. Source: Lund et al., 4th Generation District Heating (4GDH), Energy 2014; ScienceDirect topic review.
−40 °COur cold-climate designs are specified for ambient down to −40 °C.Condition: Design ambient for outdoor heat-rejection equipment and fluid selection; not a demonstrated continuous-operation record at that temperature. Source: NextGenergy design basis for cold-climate deployments.
10 kW – 1 MWThe platform is engineered across a range from single high-density racks to megawatt-class pods.Condition: Range of thermal design points, not a single product rating. Each deployment is rated at its own supply temperature, flow and approach. Source: NextGenergy platform design envelope.
Evidence

Ten places a liquid loop can leak. Ten records that should exist when it is handed over.

Most turnover packages say "leak detection installed". Ours answers three questions for every boundary: was it tested, against what acceptance criteria, and where is the record.

The ten leak pointsThe turnover package
01Cold plate jointstested · criteria · record
02Quick disconnectstested · criteria · record
03Hose crimpstested · criteria · record
04Manifold branchestested · criteria · record
05Elastomeric sealstested · criteria · record
06Threaded and compression fittingstested · criteria · record
07CDU internal boundariestested · criteria · record
08Field welds and hot worktested · criteria · record
09Balancing and isolation valvestested · criteria · record
10Fill, drain, vent and sample portstested · criteria · record
